teaching_cases.assumptions: Original fictional example. Five statements posted at a town library noticeboard: (1) "Sunday opening hours" — a topic phrase; nothing is asserted, no one can disagree. activities.title: Label flyer statements
activities.instructions:
Original fictional flyer. A town library fundraising flyer includes these four statements:

A. "The library's reading room"
B. "The council should fund weekend tutoring"
C. "Weekend tutoring raised attendance"
D. "The reading room matters to families"

Recall the cue from the worked example: a statement is a claim when a reader could reasonably reply "I disagree" — it takes a disputable position, whether about policy ("should"), fact ("rose", "raised"), or value ("matters"). A topic only names a subject and cannot be disagreed with.

Label each statement A–D as a topic or a claim. For each claim, quote the word or phrase that does the asserting (the deciding cue someone would reject). For each topic, say in a few words why nothing is asserted. Note: a value statement like "matters" cannot be dismissed as a mere topic just because it has no measurable test — it still asserts something someone could dispute.

fields.label: Your four labels with quoted cues (A–D)
criteria: Labels A and D as topics and B and C as claims (or gives a reasoned alternative accepted in the explanation)
Quotes the actual asserting phrase for each claim, such as "should fund weekend tutoring" and "raised attendance"
Explains that topics A and D name a subject without taking a position — or, if D is labelled a claim, quotes "matters" as a disputable value position
Does not relabel a policy or value claim as a topic for lacking a measurable test

activities.hint: For each statement, ask whether a reader could say "No, that's wrong." If yes, find the words that carry the position; if no, it only names a subject.

steps.explanation: Model answer: A — topic; it names the reading room, asserting nothing. B — claim; the cue is "should fund weekend tutoring," a policy position a councillor could reject. C — claim; the cue is "raised attendance," a factual assertion someone could dispute by pointing to other causes or flat figures. D — claim; the cue is "matters to families," a value assertion a critic could deny by saying families manage without it. Accept D labelled as a topic only if the reasoning clearly states why no position is taken; but "matters" asserts value, so the stronger answer treats D as a claim. The recurring misconception is treating value statements as non-claims because they cannot be measured — the cue is disputability, not testability.

activities.title: Judge five sentences in a letter about the library van
activities.instructions:
Original fictional letter, printed in a community newspaper.

"Dear Editor,
Our neighbourhood lost its branch library, and many of us now travel a long way to borrow a book. The mobile library van deserves more support from the town. The van's route schedule was posted at the community hall last spring. Extending the van's evening stops would help residents who work during the day. The cost of diesel for the van. Yours faithfully, a regular borrower."

Your task has two parts. First, label each of the five sentences below as a topic or a claim, quoting the word or phrase that decides it. Use the cue you practised: a claim takes a position a reader could reasonably reject; a topic only names a subject.

The five sentences to label:
A. Our neighbourhood lost its branch library.
B. The mobile library van deserves more support from the town.
C. The van's route schedule was posted at the community hall last spring.
D. Extending the van's evening stops would help residents who work during the day.
E. The cost of diesel for the van.

Second, choose the two sentences you found hardest to judge, and for each give a one-line reason your label is right, naming what a reader could or could not reject. If you think a sentence is genuinely arguable either way, say so and defend your label.

criteria: Labels each of the five sentences A–E as topic or claim with a quoted deciding cue

B is a claim, cue "deserves more support from the town" — someone could reply "No, it doesn't." numbered_draft.title: Sort a letter's sentences
numbered_draft.instructions:
Original fictional letter to a community newspaper, written by a resident named Ines.

"Dear Editor: I write about the mobile library van. (1) The mobile library van serves our village each week. (2) The van's route matters to isolated readers. (3) Reading habits in rural areas. (4) The council should keep the van's funding in next year's budget. (5) The van's book borrowing doubled after the route added our village."

Your task: label each numbered sentence as a topic or a claim. Quote the deciding word or phrase for each label, as in the noticeboard examples. Then, for the two hardest sentences — the ones you found closest to the line — add one short line each explaining why the sentence is or is not a position someone could reasonably reject.
numbered_draft.hint: For each sentence, ask whether a reader could say "I disagree" and point at the exact words that make that possible.

fields.label: Your five labels with quoted cues and two reasons
criteria: Labels each of the five sentences as topic or claim, quoting the deciding phrase
Treats (2) and (5) as claims: a value claim and a factual claim, not topics, despite lacking a policy test or being factual
Treats (3) as a topic because it only names a subject and takes no position; treats (1) as a claim or, if labelled a topic, explains why a plain report is not asserted as disputable
Gives a one-line reason for the two hardest sentences that invokes the disputable-position cue rather than sentence length or grammar
Where a sentence is a claim, quotes the asserting phrase (e.g. "matters", "doubled", "should keep") rather than a neutral subject phrase
fields.explanation: Sentences (2), (4) and (5) are claims: "matters to isolated readers" asserts value, "should keep the van's funding" asserts policy, and "borrowing doubled" asserts a disputable fact — each could be met with "I disagree" and each needs support. Sentence (3) is a bare topic: it names a subject without asserting anything. Sentence (1) sits closest to the line: read as the writer's report of fact it is a claim someone could dispute ("No, it doesn't"), though a reasoned case for treating a neutral descriptive note as a topic is acceptable if explained. A key error is relabelling (2) or (5) as topics because a value claim cannot be measured or because a factual claim "is just a fact": both are positions a reader could reject, so both need evidence, while a topic only names a subject.
